decks.title: National Income and Related Aggregates — Part 1: Concepts, Circular Flow and Methods
goals: Distinguish consumption and capital goods, final and intermediate goods, stocks and flows, gross and net investment
Explain the circular flow of income in a two-sector economy
Calculate national income by the value added, income and expenditure methods, with their precautions

slides.heading: National Income and Related Aggregates
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **basic concepts**, the **circular flow** of income, and the **three methods** of measuring national income.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: basic concepts, the circular flow of income, then the product, income and expenditure methods
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to Class 12 macroeconomics. Every year newspapers report how much the Indian economy produced and how fast it grew. Behind those headlines is national income accounting. In this first part we learn the basic words economists use, see how income goes round and round between households and firms, and practise the three ways of measuring national income.

slides.heading: What is macroeconomics?
bullets: **Microeconomics** studies single units: one consumer, one firm, the price of one good.
**Macroeconomics** studies the economy **as a whole**: national income, total output, employment, the general price level.
It asks: how much does the country produce, why do incomes rise or fall, how can the government keep prices stable?
slides.narration: Microeconomics looks at the trees: one buyer, one seller, one market. Macroeconomics looks at the forest: the total output, total employment and general level of prices in the whole economy. It deals with aggregates, which simply means totals. National income is the most important of these aggregates, so it is where we begin.

slides.heading: Kinds of goods

rows: Rice, a shirt, a haircut bought by a family
Used to produce other goods for years
A loom in a Varanasi weaving shed
Bought for final use (consumption or investment)
Paint bought by a family to paint its home
Used up or resold in production within the year
Paint bought by a builder for flats he will sell

visual.alt: Table of kinds of goods: consumption goods satisfy wants directly, capital goods produce other goods for years, final goods are bought for final use, and intermediate goods are used up in production; paint is final for a family and intermediate for a builder
visual.caption: The same good can be final or intermediate: what matters is its end use.

slides.narration: Goods can be classified in two ways. Consumption goods satisfy our wants directly, while capital goods, like a loom, help produce other goods for many years. Next, final goods are bought for final use, while intermediate goods are used up in production within the year. Look at the paint. A family painting its home buys a final good. A builder painting flats for sale buys an intermediate good. End use decides.

slides.heading: Quick check: final or intermediate?
slides.body_md: Decide by the **end use** of the good.
slides.narration: Ask what the buyer will do with the milk. Will it be consumed, or will it be used up in making something else for sale?

slides.heading: Stocks and flows
columns:
**Stock**

- Measured **at a point of time**.
- Example: capital of a firm on 31 March; wealth; money supply on a date.

**Flow**

- Measured **over a period**.
- Example: income per year; investment; depreciation; consumption.

rows: Capital, wealth, money supply on a date

visual.alt: Table comparing stock and flow: a stock is measured at a point of time, like capital or wealth or water in a tank; a flow is measured over a period, like income, investment, depreciation, or water flowing in per minute

slides.narration: Think of a water tank. The water in the tank at noon is a stock: it is measured at one moment. The water flowing in each minute is a flow: it only makes sense per unit of time. In economics, capital and wealth are stocks, while income, investment and depreciation are flows. Flows change stocks, just as the inflow raises the level in the tank.

slides.heading: Investment and depreciation
bullets: **Gross investment**: all new capital goods (machines, buildings) plus the change in stock in a year.
**Depreciation** (consumption of fixed capital): fall in value of fixed capital due to **normal wear and tear** and **expected obsolescence**.
**Net investment** = gross investment − depreciation: the true **addition** to the capital stock.
Losses from floods or unforeseen obsolescence are **capital losses**, not depreciation.

nodes.label: minus depreciation (wear and tear, expected obsolescence)
Net investment (addition to the capital stock)

visual.alt: Flow: gross investment minus depreciation gives net investment, the addition to the capital stock
visual.caption: Gross investment = net investment + depreciation

slides.narration: When firms buy new machines and buildings, that is gross investment. But some old machines wear out during the year, and some become out of date in an expected way. That loss is depreciation, also called consumption of fixed capital. Subtract it, and you get net investment, which is the real addition to the country's capital stock. Sudden losses from a flood are not depreciation.

slides.heading: Quick check: stock or flow?
slides.body_md: Look for a **time period** in the definition.
slides.narration: For each option, ask whether it would make sense to say per year. If it does, it is a flow.

slides.heading: The circular flow of income
bullets: Assume: only households and firms; households spend all income; no government, no foreign trade.

visual.caption: Two-sector circular flow: real and money flows move in opposite directions.

slides.narration: Here is a simple economy with only households and firms. Households own land, labour, capital and enterprise, and supply these factor services to firms. Firms pay them rent, wages, interest and profit. Households spend this income on the goods and services of firms. The solid outer loop shows real flows, and the dashed inner loop shows money flows, moving in the opposite direction.

slides.heading: Three points of measurement
slides.body_md: The same flow can be measured where it is **produced**, where it is **earned** and where it is **spent**.

nodes.label: Income: value added paid out as rent, wages, interest, profit
Expenditure: households spend income on final goods

visual.alt: Flow of the three points of measurement: production, where firms add value; income, where value added is paid out as factor incomes; and expenditure, where incomes are spent on final goods and return to firms
visual.caption: Product = Income = Expenditure

slides.narration: Because income goes round in a circle, we can stand at three different points and measure it. At the production point we add up the value added by firms. At the income point we add up rent, wages, interest and profit. At the expenditure point we add up spending on final goods. In a two-sector economy all three totals are the same, which gives us three methods.

slides.heading: Quick check: real or money flow?
slides.body_md: Real flows are things; money flows are payments.
slides.narration: Remember the two loops in the diagram. One carries factor services and goods, the other carries payments.

slides.heading: Product method and double counting
bullets: **Value of output** = sales + change in stock.
**Gross value added at MP** = value of output − intermediate consumption.
Adding sales of every stage counts inputs again and again: **double counting**.

visual.alt: Table of a cotton–yarn–shirt chain: sales of 300, 500 and 900 rupees; values added 300, 200 and 400; adding sales gives 1,700, which double counts, while total value added is 900, equal to the final shirts
visual.caption: Add values added, not sales.

slides.narration: In the product method we add the value added by every producer. Look at the shirt chain. If we added all three sales, we would count the cotton three times and the yarn twice, getting 1,700. Adding only the value added at each stage gives 900, exactly the value of the final shirts. So the product method avoids double counting by design.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: value added by a firm
slides.body_md: An imagined spinning mill in Coimbatore (₹ lakh): sales 900, change in stock +60, intermediate consumption 400, depreciation 40, net indirect taxes 20. Find NVA at FC.
bullets: Step 1 — Output = sales + change in stock.
Step 2 — Subtract intermediate consumption for GVA at MP.
Step 3 — Subtract depreciation, then net indirect taxes.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 1: value of output 900 plus 60 equals 960; gross value added at market price 960 minus 400 equals 560; net value added at market price 520; net value added at factor cost 500 lakh rupees

slides.narration: First the value of output. The mill sold 900 and added 60 to its stock, so it produced 960. Subtract the 400 of cotton and power it used up, and gross value added at market price is 560. Subtract depreciation of 40 to get 520, and net indirect taxes of 20 to reach net value added at factor cost of 500 lakh rupees.

slides.heading: Income method

rows: Wages and salaries in cash, payments in kind (free meals, housing), employer's contribution to social security
Rent and royalty, interest, profit (dividends + corporate tax + retained earnings)
Earnings of farmers, shopkeepers, doctors in private practice, where labour and capital returns cannot be separated
**NDP at factor cost (domestic income)**; add NFIA for national income

visual.alt: Table of the income method: compensation of employees, operating surplus made of rent, interest and profit, and mixed income of the self-employed add up to net domestic product at factor cost

slides.narration: In the income method we add the factor incomes paid out by all producers. Compensation of employees includes wages, payments in kind like free meals, and the employer's contribution to social security. Operating surplus is rent, interest and profit. Mixed income belongs to the self-employed, such as a farmer or shopkeeper, whose returns cannot be split. Their sum is domestic income.

slides.heading: Expenditure method

rows: Firms and others: fixed capital + change in stock
Rest of the world: exports − imports

visual.alt: Table of the expenditure method: private consumption, government consumption, gross domestic capital formation and net exports add up to gross domestic product at market price

slides.narration: In the expenditure method we add all spending on final goods and services produced in the country. Households spend on consumption, the government on its final consumption, firms on new capital goods and stocks, and foreigners on our exports. Imports are subtracted because that spending goes to production abroad. The total is gross domestic product at market price.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: expenditure method
slides.body_md: Imagined economy (₹ crore): C 1,200, I 300, G 250, exports 150, imports 200.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 2: consumption 1,200, investment 300, government 250 and net exports minus 50 give GDP at market price of 1,700 crore rupees

slides.narration: Add the four parts. Consumption 1,200, investment 300 and government spending 250 make 1,750. Exports of 150 minus imports of 200 give net exports of minus 50. So GDP at market price is 1,700 crore rupees. Notice that net exports can be negative, and that only final spending is included.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: income method
slides.body_md: Same imagined economy, viewed from the income side (₹ crore).

visual.alt: Table of worked example 3: compensation of employees 800, operating surplus 420 and mixed income 300 give NDP at factor cost of 1,520 crore rupees

slides.narration: Now add factor incomes. Compensation of employees is 800. Rent 120, interest 90 and profit 210 together make an operating surplus of 420. Mixed income of the self-employed is 300. The total, 1,520, is net domestic product at factor cost, because factor incomes contain neither depreciation nor indirect taxes. We will meet this number again in Part 2.

slides.heading: What is counted, and what is not

rows: Imputed rent of an owner-occupied house
Grain kept by a farmer for his family

visual.alt: Checklist table: imputed rent, own-account production and payments in kind are counted; transfers, second-hand goods, shares and bonds, unpaid housework and lottery prizes are not, though commissions and brokerage are

slides.narration: Here is your checklist. Count anything that is a payment for current production: imputed rent of owner-occupied houses, grain a farmer keeps for his family, and meals given free to staff. Leave out transfers like pensions and scholarships, second-hand goods and shares, because nothing new is produced. But the dealer's commission and the broker's fee are current services, so they are counted.

slides.heading: Quick check: value added
slides.body_md: Which formula gives gross value added?
slides.narration: Think back to the spinning mill and the order of the steps you used.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Output − intermediate consumption of every firm

visual.alt: Summary table of the three methods: the product method adds values added and gives GDP at market price; the income method adds factor incomes and gives NDP at factor cost; the expenditure method adds final expenditures and gives GDP at market price

slides.narration: To sum up: goods are classified by their use; stocks are measured at a point of time and flows over a period; net investment is gross investment minus depreciation. Income flows in a circle between households and firms, so we can measure it by value added, by factor incomes or by final expenditure, taking care to avoid double counting and transfers.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Final vs intermediate: always argue from **end use**, with the buyer named.
Write **value of output = sales + change in stock** before anything else; a fall in stock is negative.
Show every **step and formula** in numericals: marks are given for steps, not just the answer.
In "included or not" questions, the **reason** earns the mark.
Never add **transfer payments** or **second-hand sales**; do add commissions.
slides.narration: Some advice for the board exam. In numericals, write the formula first, then substitute, then give the answer with its unit. Many students forget that a fall in stock is negative. In questions on what to include, the mark is for the reason, so always say why. And remember that the commission on a second-hand sale is counted, though the sale itself is not.

decks.title: National Income and Related Aggregates — Part 2: Aggregates, Real GDP and Welfare
goals: Explain domestic territory, normal residents and net factor income from abroad
Convert between GDP, GNP, NDP and NNP at market price and factor cost
Distinguish real and nominal GDP, calculate the GDP deflator, and evaluate GDP as an index of welfare

slides.heading: From GDP to national income
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **aggregates**, **real versus nominal GDP**, and whether **GDP measures welfare**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: three pairs of concepts, domestic territory and residents, the conversion from GDP to national income, real and nominal GDP, and GDP and welfare
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 1 we measured GDP. But GDP is only one of eight related aggregates. In this part we learn the three pairs of ideas behind them, convert GDP into national income step by step, separate real growth from price rises, and finally ask a big question: does a higher GDP always mean that people are better off?

slides.heading: Three pairs of concepts

rows: Market price includes net indirect taxes

visual.alt: Table of the three pairs of concepts: gross and net differ by depreciation, domestic and national by net factor income from abroad, market price and factor cost by net indirect taxes

slides.narration: Every aggregate name is built from three choices. Gross or net: gross includes depreciation, net does not. Domestic or national: domestic is about the territory, national is about the normal residents. Market price or factor cost: market price includes indirect taxes minus subsidies. Two choices for each of three pairs give eight aggregates, such as GDP at market price or NNP at factor cost.

slides.heading: Domestic territory and normal residents
bullets: **Normal resident:** a person or institution that ordinarily lives in a country and whose **centre of economic interest** lies there, usually for a year or more.

rows: Land, territorial waters and airspace of India
Foreign embassies and consulates in India
Indian embassies, consulates and military bases abroad
Offices of international organisations in India
Ships, aircraft and fishing boats run by residents between countries or in international waters
Factories of Indian companies located abroad

visual.alt: Table of domestic territory: it includes the land, waters and airspace of India, Indian embassies abroad and ships, aircraft and fishing boats run by residents; it excludes foreign embassies and international organisations in India and factories of Indian companies abroad

slides.narration: Domestic territory is more than the map. It includes Indian embassies abroad and ships, planes and fishing boats run by Indian residents. But foreign embassies and offices of international organisations in India are not part of it. A normal resident is someone who ordinarily lives in the country and has their economic interest there. Citizenship does not decide it.

slides.heading: Quick check: who is a normal resident?
slides.body_md: Think of where the person ordinarily lives and earns.
slides.narration: Remember: residence is about where one ordinarily lives and has economic interest, not about the passport.

slides.heading: Net factor income from abroad
bullets: NFIA = factor income earned by residents from abroad − factor income paid to non-residents.
National income = domestic income + NFIA.

nodes.label: Factor income earned by residents from abroad
minus factor income paid to non-residents

visual.alt: Flow: factor income earned from abroad minus factor income paid to non-residents is net factor income from abroad, which is added to domestic income to give national income
visual.caption: NFIA can be positive or negative

slides.narration: Indian engineers working abroad and Indian firms with factories overseas earn factor income from the rest of the world. At the same time, foreign workers and investors earn income in India and send it home. The difference is net factor income from abroad. It can be positive or negative. Adding it to domestic income gives national income.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: GDP at MP to national income
slides.body_md: Imagined economy (₹ crore): GDP at MP 1,700, depreciation 100, net indirect taxes 120, NFIA -30.

nodes.label: − net indirect taxes 120 → NDP at FC (1,480)
+ NFIA (-30) → NNP at FC = national income (1,450)

visual.alt: Ladder from GDP at market price 1,700 to NDP at market price 1,600 after depreciation, to NDP at factor cost 1,480 after net indirect taxes, to national income 1,450 after adding net factor income from abroad of minus 30
visual.caption: Worked example 4 (₹ crore, imagined)

slides.narration: Take the GDP of 1,700 from Part 1. Subtract depreciation of 100 to get NDP at market price of 1,600. Subtract net indirect taxes of 120 to reach NDP at factor cost of 1,480. Finally add net factor income from abroad, which is minus 30, to get national income of 1,450 crore rupees. The order of the three steps can change; the answer does not.

slides.heading: Market price and factor cost
bullets: **Net indirect taxes** = indirect taxes − subsidies.
FC = MP − NIT; if subsidies exceed indirect taxes, FC is higher than MP.

visual.alt: Table of a bicycle price: factor cost 4,000 rupees plus indirect taxes 480 minus a subsidy of 80 gives a market price of 4,400 rupees
visual.caption: Market price = factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies.

slides.narration: The price you pay in a shop is the market price. It includes indirect taxes such as GST, and it is lowered by any subsidy. What the factors of production receive is the factor cost. So factor cost equals market price minus net indirect taxes. In the bicycle example, the factors get 4,000 rupees, but the buyer pays 4,400.

slides.heading: Quick check: which aggregate is national income?
slides.body_md: Gross or net? Domestic or national? Market price or factor cost?
slides.narration: Go through the three pairs one by one and pick the right choice in each.

slides.heading: Nominal and real GDP
columns:
**Nominal GDP**

- Output valued at **current-year prices**.
- Rises if output rises **or** prices rise.

**Real GDP**

- Output valued at **base-year prices**.
- Rises **only** if output rises.

visual.caption: Nominal GDP grew 35.4 per cent, real GDP only 19.2 per cent.

slides.narration: Suppose the bills of a town rise because prices have gone up. Has the town produced more? Not necessarily. Nominal GDP uses current prices, so it rises with prices as well as output. Real GDP uses the prices of a fixed base year, so it rises only when more goods and services are produced. For growth, economists use real GDP.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: real GDP and the deflator
slides.body_md: An imagined town produces only mangoes and bicycles; base year 2020.
bullets: GDP deflator = (nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 5: GDP in 2020 is 1,30,000 rupees; 2024 nominal GDP is 1,76,000 rupees; 2024 real GDP at 2020 prices is 1,55,000 rupees
visual.caption: Deflator 2024 = 1,76,000 ÷ 1,55,000 × 100 ≈ 113.5

slides.narration: In 2024 the town's output at 2024 prices is 1,76,000 rupees. That is nominal GDP. Valued at 2020 prices, the same output is worth 1,55,000 rupees. That is real GDP. Divide nominal by real and multiply by 100: the deflator is about 113.5, so prices rose by about 13.5 per cent. Nominal GDP grew about 35 per cent, but real output grew only about 19 per cent.

slides.heading: The GDP deflator
bullets: A **price index** for everything produced in the country, not just a consumer basket.
Deflator above 100: prices have **risen** since the base year.
Real GDP = (nominal GDP ÷ deflator) × 100.
slides.narration: The GDP deflator is a price index for all goods and services produced in the economy. If it is 120, prices on average are 20 per cent higher than in the base year. Turn the formula around and you can find real GDP from nominal GDP and the deflator. This is how growth figures are cleaned of inflation.

Second, non-monetary exchanges such as unpaid care at home are not counted. Third, externalities: GDP does not subtract harm from pollution or add benefits like a public park.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Three pairs of ideas build eight aggregates. Subtract depreciation to go from gross to net, add NFIA to go from domestic to national, and subtract net indirect taxes to go from market price to factor cost. National income is NNP at factor cost. Real GDP removes price changes, the deflator measures them, and GDP is only a partial measure of welfare.

Deflator answers have **no unit**; real and nominal GDP are in rupees.
slides.narration: Common mistakes cost easy marks. Students mix up net factor income to abroad and from abroad, or forget that subsidies are subtracted from indirect taxes. sections.heading: 1. Basic concepts
sections.body_md:
**Macroeconomics** studies the economy as a whole through aggregates: national income, output, employment, the general price level.

- **Consumption goods** satisfy wants directly (food, clothes, services). **Capital goods** are fixed assets used in production for many years (machines, buildings, tools).
- **Final goods** are bought for final use (consumption or investment) and are not used up or resold in production in the year. **Intermediate goods** are used up as raw materials or resold. The classification depends on **end use**: sugar for a household is final, sugar for a sweet shop is intermediate.
- **Stocks** are measured at a point of time (capital, wealth); **flows** over a period (income, investment, depreciation). Flows change stocks.
- **Gross investment** = addition to capital goods and stocks in a year; **depreciation** (consumption of fixed capital) = loss in value from normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence; **net investment** = gross investment − depreciation.

sections.heading: 2. Circular flow of income (two-sector model)
sections.body_md:
**Assumptions:** only households and firms; households spend all their income on consumption (no saving); firms sell all output to households; no government and no foreign trade.

**Real flows:** factor services from households to firms; goods and services from firms to households.

**Money flows:** factor payments (rent, wages, interest, profit) from firms to households; consumption expenditure from households to firms.

Real and money flows move in opposite directions. Because the whole value of output is paid out as factor incomes and all income is spent on output, **value of output = factor income = expenditure**. This is why national income can be measured by three methods.

sections.heading: 3. Value added (product) method
sections.body_md:
1. **Value of output** = sales + change in stock (closing stock − opening stock).
2. **GVA at MP** = value of output − intermediate consumption.
3. **NVA at MP** = GVA at MP − depreciation; **NVA at FC** = NVA at MP − net indirect taxes.
4. Sum of GVA at MP of all producers in the domestic territory = **GDP at MP**.

**Double counting** happens when the value of intermediate goods is counted again inside final goods. Avoid it by adding only values added (or only final goods).

**Precautions:** include **own-account production** (grain kept for the family) and **imputed rent** of owner-occupied houses; exclude **sale of second-hand goods** (but include the commission), and exclude **intermediate goods**; exclude unpaid household services.

sections.heading: 4. Income and expenditure methods
sections.body_md:
**Income method:** NDP at FC = **compensation of employees** (wages in cash and kind, employer's social security contribution) + **operating surplus** (rent and royalty, interest, profit) + **mixed income of the self-employed**. Add NFIA for national income.
- Exclude **transfer incomes** (pensions, scholarships, gifts), **windfall gains** (lottery) and **capital gains** on sale of assets.
- Include income in kind and imputed rent.

**Expenditure method:** GDP at MP = **private final consumption expenditure** + **government final consumption expenditure** + **gross domestic capital formation** (fixed capital + change in stock) + **net exports** (X − M).
- Exclude spending on **intermediate goods**, **second-hand goods**, **financial assets** (shares, bonds) and **transfer payments**.

sections.heading: 6. Real and nominal GDP, the deflator, and welfare
sections.body_md:
- **Nominal GDP:** output valued at current prices. **Real GDP:** output valued at base-year (constant) prices; it changes only when output changes.
- **GDP deflator** = (nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100: a price index for all goods and services produced.
- **Real GDP** = (nominal GDP ÷ deflator) × 100.

**GDP and welfare.** Welfare is the well-being of people. GDP is an imperfect index because of:
1. **Distribution of GDP:** growth may benefit a few.
2. **Non-monetary exchanges:** unpaid domestic work and barter are not counted.
3. **Externalities:** harm (pollution) is not subtracted and benefits (a public garden) are not added.

A rise in real GDP is therefore a useful but incomplete sign of a rise in welfare.

questions.stem_md: Macroeconomics studies the economy

options.text_md: through the choices of a single consumer or a single firm
as a whole, through aggregates such as national income, total employment and the general price level
only through the prices of individual goods
only through the accounts of the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** as a whole, through aggregates such as national income, total employment and the general price level. Macroeconomics deals with aggregates of the whole economy. Single consumers, firms and individual prices are the subject of microeconomics; government accounts are only one part of the economy.

questions.stem_md: Whether a good is classified as a **final** good or an **intermediate** good depends on

options.text_md: its physical nature, such as size or weight
its price in the market
whether it is produced by a large or a small firm
the use to which it is put by its buyer

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the use to which it is put by its buyer. The same good can be final or intermediate: milk bought by a family is final, milk bought by a sweet shop is intermediate. So the test is end use, not nature, price or size of the producer.

questions.stem_md: Gurpreet, a farmer near Ludhiana, buys a new tractor to plough his fields for the next ten years. The tractor is

options.text_md: a final good and a capital good
an intermediate good, because it helps produce wheat
a consumption good, because the farmer buys it
neither final nor intermediate, because it is not resold

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a final good and a capital good. A tractor is used again and again in production and is not used up or resold within the year, so it is a capital good, and capital goods are final goods. It is not intermediate (that would need it to be used up in one cycle) and it does not satisfy a consumer want directly.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an **intermediate** good?

options.text_md: A car bought by a family in Pune
A welding machine bought by a car maker
Steel sheets bought by a car maker in Pune
Steel utensils bought by a household

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Steel sheets bought by a car maker in Pune. Steel sheets are used up in making cars within the year and are resold as part of the car, so they are intermediate. The family car and household utensils are consumption goods, and the welding machine is a capital good; all three are final goods.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a **flow** variable?

options.text_md: The capital stock of a country on 31 March
The wealth of a family
National income of a year
The money supply on a given date

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** National income of a year. National income is measured over a period (a year), so it is a flow. Capital stock, wealth and money supply on a date are measured at a point of time, so they are stocks.

questions.stem_md: Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) is the fall in the value of fixed capital caused by

options.text_md: normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence
a flood or an earthquake
a sudden change in technology that nobody expected
a fall in the share price of the company

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence. Depreciation is the expected loss: normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence. Losses from natural disasters or unforeseen obsolescence are capital losses, and share prices are not about the physical capital used in production.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Machines bought by a firm for its own use are treated as final goods.

**Reason (R):** Machines are not used up or resold during the year; they are used repeatedly in production over many years.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Machines are final goods because they are not transformed or used up within the accounting year, which is exactly what R states, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Income is a flow variable.

**Reason (R):** Income is measured at a particular point of time.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: income has a time dimension (per month, per year). R is false: being measured at a point of time is what defines a stock, not a flow.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Milk bought by a sweet shop in Kolkata to make rasgullas for sale is a final good.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The sweet shop uses the milk up in making rasgullas, which it then sells, so the milk is an intermediate good here. Milk bought by a family for drinking would be final.

questions.stem_md: Net investment = gross investment − ___.
questions.solution_md: Net investment is gross investment minus depreciation (consumption of fixed capital).

questions.stem_md: An imagined economy's gross investment in a year is ₹840 crore and depreciation is ₹95 crore. Find net investment (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Net investment = gross investment − depreciation.
Step 2: 840 − 95 = 745. So ₹745 crore.

questions.stem_md: Match each variable with its correct description.

options.text_md: Capital of a firm on 31 March
Investment during a year
Wear and tear of machines
Unsold goods added to stock in a year

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Capital on a date is a stock; investment per year is a flow; normal wear and tear is depreciation; the addition to unsold goods in a year is the change in stock, a part of investment.

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference between final goods and intermediate goods, using the example of sugar.
questions.solution_md: Define both by end use and show that the same good (sugar) can be either.

answer.model_answer_md: **Final goods** are bought for **final use** (consumption or investment) and are not resold or used up in further production in the year. **Intermediate goods** are **used up** in producing other goods. Sugar bought by a **household** for its tea is final; sugar bought by a **mithai shop** to make sweets for sale is intermediate.

marking_scheme.step: Both terms distinguished by end use

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between stock and flow variables, giving one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Point of time vs period of time, with one correct example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A **stock** is measured **at a point of time** and has no time dimension, e.g. the **capital** of a firm on 31 March. A **flow** is measured **over a period of time**, e.g. **national income** or investment per year. Flows change stocks: investment during a year adds to the capital stock.

questions.stem_md: A country's gross investment is positive, but its net investment is zero. What does this tell you about its capital stock? Explain with the relation between the two.
questions.solution_md: Use the relation, conclude that gross investment just covers depreciation, and infer that capital stock is unchanged.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Gross investment = net investment + depreciation**, so here gross investment is **equal to depreciation**.
2. All new machines and buildings only **replace** the capital that was **worn out** during the year.
3. So the **capital stock stays the same**: the economy is not adding to its capacity to produce, even though it is spending on investment goods.

marking_scheme.step: Capital stock unchanged, capacity not growing

questions.stem_md: In the simple two-sector model of the circular flow of income, it is assumed that households

options.text_md: save a part of their income in banks
pay taxes to the government
buy some goods from other countries
spend all their income on goods and services produced by firms

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** spend all their income on goods and services produced by firms. The two-sector model has only households and firms, no saving, no government and no foreign trade, so households spend their whole income on the output of firms.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is part of the **real flow** in the circular flow of income?

options.text_md: Wages paid by firms to households
Factor services such as labour going from households to firms
Consumption expenditure by households
Profits paid to the owners of firms

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Factor services such as labour going from households to firms. The real flow is the movement of factor services and of goods and services. Wages, consumption spending and profits are money flows.

questions.stem_md: Ravi works in a biscuit factory in Kanpur and spends his salary on biscuits, clothes and rent. In the circular flow, his salary is

options.text_md: a factor payment flowing from firms to households
a real flow from households to firms
a consumption expenditure flowing from households to firms
a leakage from the circular flow

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a factor payment flowing from firms to households. A salary is a payment for labour, a factor service, so it is a factor payment (money flow) from firms to households. His spending on goods is consumption expenditure, which flows back to firms.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a two-sector economy, total factor payments, total consumption expenditure and the value of output are equal.

**Reason (R):** Firms pay out the whole value of output as factor payments, and households spend the whole of this income on the output of firms.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Because value of output is fully paid out as factor incomes and fully spent on the same output, the three totals are equal; R gives exactly this reason.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the two-sector circular flow model, firms sell a part of their output to the government.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The two-sector model has only households and firms; there is no government sector, so firms sell all output to households.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of one turn of the circular flow in a two-sector economy, starting with households.

options.text_md: Households spend this income on the goods and services of firms
Households supply land, labour, capital and enterprise to firms
Firms pay rent, wages, interest and profit to households
Firms use these factor services to produce goods and services

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Factor services go first to firms, firms produce, factor incomes are paid to households, and households spend the income on the output, which returns the money to firms.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the real flow and the money flow in the circular flow of income.
questions.solution_md: Define each flow with what moves and its direction.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Real flow:** the movement of **factor services** from households to firms and of **goods and services** from firms to households.
2. **Money flow:** the movement of **factor payments** (rent, wages, interest, profit) from firms to households and of **consumption expenditure** from households to firms. The two flow in **opposite directions**.

questions.stem_md: Using the circular flow, explain why national income can be measured at three different points and why all three give the same total.
questions.solution_md: Name the three points of the flow and argue that they measure one and the same flow.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Production point:** firms produce goods and services; adding the **value added** by all firms gives the product measure.
2. **Income point:** the whole value added is paid out as **factor incomes** (rent, wages, interest, profit); adding them gives the income measure.
3. **Expenditure point:** households spend this income on the **final goods** of firms. Since the **same flow** of money passes each point, product = income = expenditure.

marking_scheme.step: Expenditure point and why the totals are equal

questions.stem_md: Explain the circular flow of income in a two-sector economy. State its assumptions and the real and money flows.
questions.solution_md: Assumptions, the two real flows, the two money flows, and the conclusion that the totals are equal.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Assumptions:** only **two sectors**, households and firms; households **spend all** their income (no saving); **no government** and **no foreign trade**.
2. **Households** own the factors of production and supply **factor services** to firms (real flow).
3. **Firms** pay **factor payments** (rent, wages, interest, profit) to households (money flow).
4. Firms produce **goods and services** that go to households (real flow), and households pay **consumption expenditure** to firms (money flow).
5. The flows move in **opposite directions** and never stop, so **income = expenditure = value of output**: national income is a circular flow.

marking_scheme.step: Opposite directions of real and money flows

questions.stem_md: Gross value added at market price by a firm equals

options.text_md: sales plus intermediate consumption
value of output minus intermediate consumption
value of output minus depreciation
sales minus wages paid

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** value of output minus intermediate consumption. Value added is what the firm adds to the inputs it buys: value of output less intermediate consumption. Subtracting depreciation gives the net (not gross) measure; wages are a part of value added, not deducted from it.

questions.stem_md: A firm's value of output in a year is

options.text_md: sales minus change in stock
sales minus intermediate consumption
sales plus change in stock
sales plus depreciation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** sales plus change in stock. Output produced in a year is either sold or added to stock, so value of output = sales + change in stock (the change can be negative). Subtracting intermediate consumption gives value added, not output.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is **included** in the national income of India?

options.text_md: An old-age pension paid by the government
A scholarship given to a student
Money won in a lottery
Rent that the owner of a flat would have paid for living in his own flat (imputed rent)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Rent that the owner of a flat would have paid for living in his own flat (imputed rent). Owner-occupied housing is a real service produced during the year, so its imputed rent is included. Pensions and scholarships are transfer payments, and lottery winnings are windfall gains; none of these is a payment for a productive service.

questions.stem_md: Meena sells her five-year-old scooter for ₹30,000 through a dealer in Jaipur, who charges a commission of ₹1,500. What is added to this year's GDP from the deal?

options.text_md: Nothing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹1,500. The scooter was counted in GDP in the year it was made, so its resale is not new production. But the dealer's service of bringing buyer and seller together is produced this year, so only the commission of ₹1,500 is added.

questions.stem_md: The purchase of shares of a company is not included in national income because

options.text_md: shares are always bought by foreigners
shares are a capital good
it is only a transfer of ownership of a financial asset and does not create any good or service
the government taxes the purchase of shares

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** it is only a transfer of ownership of a financial asset and does not create any good or service. Buying shares or bonds changes who owns a claim; nothing is produced. (A broker's commission on the deal is a service and is counted.) The other options are untrue or irrelevant.

questions.stem_md: A self-employed tailor in Surat earns from her own labour, her own shop and her own sewing machines, and the parts cannot be separated. In the income method, her earnings are recorded as

options.text_md: compensation of employees
mixed income of the self-employed
operating surplus
transfer income

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** mixed income of the self-employed. When the returns to one's own labour, land and capital cannot be separated, the whole is mixed income of the self-employed. Compensation of employees needs an employer, and operating surplus is rent, interest and profit of enterprises.

questions.stem_md: While estimating national income by the **expenditure method**, which item is **included**?

options.text_md: Purchase of new machines by a factory
Purchase of raw cotton by a textile mill
Unemployment allowance paid by the government
Purchase of a second-hand truck

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Purchase of new machines by a factory. New machines are gross domestic capital formation, a final expenditure. Raw cotton is intermediate consumption, the allowance is a transfer, and the second-hand truck was counted when it was made.

questions.stem_md: Counting the value of an input more than once while estimating national output is called

options.text_md: depreciation
double counting
imputation
net factor income from abroad

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** double counting. Adding the value of intermediate goods again with the final good counts the same value twice: double counting. It is avoided by the value-added method or by counting final goods only.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Scholarships given by the government are not included in national income.

**Reason (R):** Scholarships are payments made to students for the productive services they render while studying.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: a scholarship is a **transfer payment**, received without any productive service in return, and that is exactly why it is excluded.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The sale of an old house is not included in the national income of the current year.

**Reason (R):** The commission earned by an estate agent on the sale of an old house is included in national income.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. A is true because the house was counted when it was built; R is a separate fact about the agent's current service.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Wheat grown by a farmer in Madhya Pradesh and kept for his family's own use is included in national income.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Production for self-consumption is real output of the year; it is valued at market prices and included (own-account production).

questions.stem_md: An imagined furniture firm in Saharanpur reports for a year (₹ lakh): sales 750, change in stock −30, purchase of wood and other inputs 420, depreciation 25, net indirect taxes 15. Find its **net value added at factor cost** (in ₹ lakh).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Value of output = sales + change in stock = 750 + (−30) = 720.
Step 2: GVA at MP = 720 − 420 = 300.
Step 3: NVA at FC = 300 − 25 − 15 = 260. So ₹260 lakh.

marking_scheme.step: Value of output and GVA at MP

questions.stem_md: For an imagined economy (₹ crore): private final consumption expenditure 2,400; gross domestic capital formation 600; government final consumption expenditure 500; exports 300; imports 380. Find GDP at market price (in ₹ crore).
For an imagined economy (₹ crore): compensation of employees 1,100; rent 150; interest 120; profit 330; mixed income of the self-employed 400. Find domestic income (NDP at factor cost) (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Operating surplus = 150 + 120 + 330 = 600.
Step 2: NDP at FC = 1,100 + 600 + 400 = 2,100. So ₹2,100 crore.

questions.stem_md: Match each item with the method of measuring national income in which it appears.

options.text_md: Intermediate consumption of a sugar mill
Mixed income of a self-employed carpenter
Government final consumption expenditure
Net exports

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Intermediate consumption is deducted from output in the value-added method; mixed income is a factor income; government consumption and net exports are components of final expenditure.

questions.stem_md: What is double counting? State two ways in which it can be avoided.
questions.solution_md: Meaning with an example, then the two approaches: final-goods approach and value-added approach.

answer.model_answer_md: **Double counting** means counting the value of a good **more than once**, for example counting both flour and the bread made from it. It is avoided by (1) counting only the value of **final goods**, or (2) adding only the **value added** at each stage of production.

questions.stem_md: Giving reasons, state whether the following are included in national income: (a) free meals given by a hotel to its staff; (b) the purchase of new shares of a company by a household.
questions.solution_md: Meals: compensation in kind. Shares: a financial transaction, not production.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) **Included**: free meals are a payment **in kind** for work, so they are part of **compensation of employees**. (b) **Excluded**: buying shares is only a **transfer of ownership** of a **financial asset**; no good or service is produced. (The dividend later earned on them is a factor income.)

questions.stem_md: An imagined spice-processing unit in Kochi has (₹ lakh): sales 900, closing stock 80, opening stock 50, purchase of raw spices and packing material 520, depreciation 30, goods and services tax paid 40, subsidy received 10. Calculate its net value added at factor cost.
questions.solution_md: Output from sales and change in stock; subtract intermediate consumption, depreciation and net indirect taxes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Change in stock = 80 − 50 = **30**; value of output = 900 + 30 = **930**.
2. GVA at MP = 930 − 520 = **410**; NVA at MP = 410 − 30 = **380**.
3. Net indirect taxes = 40 − 10 = **30**; NVA at FC = 380 − 30 = **₹350 lakh**.

questions.stem_md: State three precautions to be taken while estimating national income by the expenditure method.
questions.solution_md: Any three valid precautions, each with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Count only **final expenditure**; spending on **intermediate goods** is left out to avoid double counting.
2. Leave out **transfer payments** such as pensions, scholarships and relief, which buy no current good or service.
3. Leave out spending on **second-hand goods** and on **financial assets** (shares, bonds); they are not current production.

questions.stem_md: Explain the steps involved in estimating national income by the income method, and state two precautions.
questions.solution_md: Sectors, the three components, the sum as NDP at FC, adding NFIA, then two precautions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Classify** producing enterprises into industrial sectors (primary, secondary, tertiary).
2. Estimate the **factor incomes** paid by each sector: **compensation of employees** (wages in cash and kind, employer's social security contribution), **operating surplus** (rent, interest, profit) and **mixed income** of the self-employed.
3. Add them for all sectors to get **domestic income (NDP at FC)**.
4. Add **net factor income from abroad** to get **national income (NNP at FC)**.
5. **Precautions:** exclude **transfer incomes** and **windfall gains**; include **imputed rent** and income in kind.

questions.stem_md: An imagined economy has two firms (₹ crore). **Firm A** sells raw cotton worth 300 to Firm B and exports cotton worth 100; its change in stock is +20; it buys nothing from other firms; its depreciation is 15. **Firm B** sells cloth worth 700 to households and 150 to the government; it buys cotton worth 300 from Firm A; its change in stock is −10; its depreciation is 25. Net indirect taxes in the economy are 45. Calculate (i) GVA at MP of each firm and (ii) NDP at factor cost of the economy.
questions.solution_md: Value of output of each firm from all its sales plus change in stock, subtract intermediate consumption, add for GDP, then subtract depreciation and net indirect taxes.

questions.stem_md: From the data of an imagined economy (₹ crore), calculate national income by the expenditure method: private final consumption expenditure 3,000; government final consumption expenditure 700; net domestic fixed capital formation 500; change in stock 60; consumption of fixed capital 140; exports 250; imports 330; indirect taxes 310; subsidies 40; net factor income to abroad 50.
questions.solution_md: Build gross investment, add the four expenditures, then move to net, factor cost and national.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Gross domestic capital formation = 500 + 60 + 140 = **700**.
2. GDP at MP = 3,000 + 700 + 700 + (250 − 330) = **4,320**.
3. NDP at MP = 4,320 − 140 = **4,180**.
4. NDP at FC = 4,180 − (310 − 40) = **3,910**.
5. NNP at FC = 3,910 − 50 = **₹3,860 crore** (net factor income **to** abroad is subtracted).

questions.stem_md: Study the table and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined firms and figures, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Step 1: Value added = sales − purchases from other firms.
Step 2: 900 − 400 = 500. So ₹500 thousand.

**(b)** Step 1: Values added: 400 + 500 + 400.
Step 2: Total = 1,300. So ₹1,300 thousand.

**(c) (i)** Name double counting and show that the sum of values added equals the final sales.

**OR (c) (ii)** No: the refrigerator is gross investment, not intermediate consumption.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **500 ₹ thousand**

**(b)** **1,300 ₹ thousand**

**(c) (i)** The official has made the error of **double counting**: the leaves are counted in the factory's sales and again in the retailer's. The correct output is the total value added, **₹1,300 thousand**, which **equals** the value of the **final good** sold to households (₹1,300 thousand).

**OR (c) (ii)** **No.** A refrigerator is a **capital good** used for years; it is a **final good** (investment), not intermediate consumption. Only goods **used up** in the year (tea packets) are deducted, so the retailer's value added stays ₹400 thousand.

questions.passage_md:
**From leaf to cup: three imagined firms in Assam (₹ thousand, one year)**

| Firm | Sells to | Sales | Purchases from other firms |
|---|---|---|---|
| Green Hills tea estate | Factory | 400 | 0 |
| Brahmaputra tea factory | Retailer | 900 | 400 |
| Chai Corner retailer | Households | 1,300 | 900 |

An official adds up the three sales figures and reports the output of the chain as ₹2,600 thousand.

children.stem_md: Find the value added by the tea factory (no change in stock).
children.solution_md:
Step 1: Value added = sales − purchases from other firms.
Step 2: 900 − 400 = 500. So ₹500 thousand.

children.stem_md: Find the total value added by the three firms.
children.solution_md:
Step 1: Values added: 400 + 500 + 400.
Step 2: Total = 1,300. So ₹1,300 thousand.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): What error has the official made? Show how the correct figure compares with the value of the final good.
children.solution_md: Name double counting and show that the sum of values added equals the final sales.

answer.model_answer_md: The official has made the error of **double counting**: the leaves are counted in the factory's sales and again in the retailer's. The correct output is the total value added, **₹1,300 thousand**, which **equals** the value of the **final good** sold to households (₹1,300 thousand).

marking_scheme.step: Sum of values added = final sales

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): If the retailer also bought a new refrigerator for ₹50 thousand, would the value added of the retailer fall? Explain.
alternatives.solution_md: No: the refrigerator is gross investment, not intermediate consumption.

answer.model_answer_md: **No.** A refrigerator is a **capital good** used for years; it is a **final good** (investment), not intermediate consumption. Only goods **used up** in the year (tea packets) are deducted, so the retailer's value added stays ₹400 thousand.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: capital good is final, not intermediate

questions.stem_md: GNP at market price equals

options.text_md: GDP at market price − depreciation
GDP at market price − net indirect taxes
NDP at factor cost + depreciation
GDP at market price + net factor income from abroad

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** GDP at market price + net factor income from abroad. Moving from domestic to national adds net factor income from abroad. Subtracting depreciation gives net measures, and subtracting net indirect taxes gives factor-cost measures.

questions.stem_md: National income is the same as

options.text_md: net national product at factor cost
gross domestic product at market price
net domestic product at market price
gross national product at factor cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** net national product at factor cost. National income is NNP at factor cost: the factor incomes earned by normal residents of a country, net of depreciation.

questions.stem_md: Net indirect taxes are

options.text_md: indirect taxes plus subsidies
direct taxes minus indirect taxes
indirect taxes minus subsidies
indirect taxes minus depreciation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** indirect taxes minus subsidies. Market price = factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies, so the gap between the two is indirect taxes minus subsidies.

questions.stem_md: GDP equals GNP when

options.text_md: depreciation is zero
indirect taxes equal subsidies
net factor income from abroad is zero
exports equal imports

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** net factor income from abroad is zero. GNP = GDP + NFIA, so they are equal when NFIA is zero (for example in a closed economy). Depreciation and net indirect taxes change net and factor-cost measures, and net exports are a part of GDP itself.

questions.stem_md: Which of these incomes is part of the **domestic** income of India?

options.text_md: Salary of a Japanese engineer working for a factory in Gujarat
Salary of an Indian doctor working in a hospital in Dubai
Rent received by an Indian resident from a flat in London
Profit of the Japanese embassy canteen in New Delhi

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Salary of a Japanese engineer working for a factory in Gujarat. Domestic income counts factor income earned within the domestic territory, whoever earns it: the factory in Gujarat is inside it. Dubai and London are outside it, and a foreign embassy in India is part of that foreign country's domestic territory.

questions.stem_md: A normal resident of a country is a person or institution who

options.text_md: is a citizen of that country, wherever he lives
has visited the country at least once in the year
pays income tax only in that country
ordinarily resides in that country and whose centre of economic interest lies there

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ordinarily resides in that country and whose centre of economic interest lies there. Residence is about where one ordinarily lives and has economic interest (usually for a year or more), not citizenship, a single visit or where one pays tax.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The GNP of a country can be lower than its GDP.

**Reason (R):** NNP is obtained by subtracting depreciation from GNP.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. GNP falls below GDP when net factor income from abroad is negative (GNP = GDP + NFIA); depreciation separates gross from net, not domestic from national.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If subsidies exceed indirect taxes, GDP at market price will be greater than GDP at factor cost.

**Reason (R):** GDP at market price = GDP at factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** R is true. With subsidies larger than indirect taxes, net indirect taxes are negative, so market price is **less** than factor cost: A is false.

questions.stem_md: NNP at market price − net indirect taxes = NNP at ___ cost.
questions.solution_md: Removing net indirect taxes from a market-price aggregate gives the factor cost aggregate.

questions.stem_md: Normal residents of an imagined country earn ₹260 crore of factor income from abroad, and the country pays ₹310 crore of factor income to non-residents. Find its net factor income from abroad (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: NFIA = factor income from abroad − factor income to abroad.
Step 2: 260 − 310 = -50. So −₹50 crore (negative).

questions.stem_md: GDP at factor cost of an imagined economy is ₹1,250 crore, indirect taxes are ₹90 crore and subsidies ₹140 crore. Find GDP at market price (in ₹ crore).
Match each conversion with the item it needs.

options.text_md: Gross to net
Domestic to national
Market price to factor cost
GDP at MP to NNP at FC

match_right.text_md: Subtract depreciation and net indirect taxes, add NFIA
Add net factor income from abroad

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(r), (c)–(q), (d)–(p). Each word of an aggregate has its own adjustment: gross–net (depreciation), domestic–national (NFIA), market price–factor cost (net indirect taxes); the last pair uses all three.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between domestic income and national income.
questions.solution_md: Territory basis vs residents basis, linked by NFIA.

answer.model_answer_md: **Domestic income (NDP at FC)** is the factor income generated **within the domestic territory** of a country, by residents and non-residents. **National income (NNP at FC)** is the factor income earned by the **normal residents** of a country, within it and abroad. National income = domestic income + **net factor income from abroad**.

marking_scheme.step: National income: residents basis, link through NFIA

questions.stem_md: Why is GDP at market price usually higher than GDP at factor cost? When could it be lower?
questions.solution_md: Explain the link through net indirect taxes and the case of large subsidies.

answer.model_answer_md: Market prices include **indirect taxes** (such as GST) and are reduced by **subsidies**: MP = FC + **net indirect taxes**. Usually indirect taxes exceed subsidies, so MP is **higher**. If **subsidies exceed indirect taxes**, NIT is negative and MP is **lower** than FC.

marking_scheme.step: Case where subsidies exceed indirect taxes

questions.stem_md: Giving reasons, state whether these are part of the domestic territory of India: (a) a fishing boat of an Indian company in international waters; (b) the office of an international organisation in New Delhi.
questions.solution_md: Apply the definition of domestic territory to each case.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) **Yes.** Ships, aircraft and fishing vessels **operated by residents** in international waters or between countries are part of the domestic territory. (b) **No.** Offices of **international organisations** in a country are **not** part of its domestic territory.

questions.stem_md: For an imagined country (₹ crore): GDP at MP 5,000; net factor income from abroad -60; consumption of fixed capital 300; indirect taxes 420; subsidies 70. Calculate (i) GNP at MP and (ii) national income.
questions.solution_md: Add NFIA, subtract depreciation, subtract net indirect taxes.

questions.stem_md: Explain the three pairs of concepts used to build national income aggregates (gross–net, domestic–national, market price–factor cost), and show how GDP at market price is converted into national income.
questions.solution_md: Each pair with its adjustment, then the chain from GDP at MP to NNP at FC.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Gross and net:** gross includes **depreciation**; net = gross − depreciation.
2. **Domestic and national:** domestic is income within the **domestic territory**; national is income of **normal residents**; national = domestic + **NFIA**.
3. **Market price and factor cost:** market price includes **net indirect taxes**; factor cost = market price − (indirect taxes − subsidies).
4. **Conversion:** start from **GDP at MP**, subtract depreciation (NDP at MP), add NFIA (NNP at MP), subtract NIT.
5. The result is **NNP at FC = national income** = GDP at MP − depreciation + NFIA − NIT.

questions.stem_md: Real GDP measures the output of a year at

options.text_md: the prices of the current year
the prices of a base year
factor cost only
world prices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the prices of a base year. Real GDP values current output at constant (base-year) prices, so it changes only when output changes. Nominal GDP uses current prices.

questions.stem_md: Nominal GDP of an imagined economy is ₹1,500 crore and real GDP is ₹1,250 crore. The GDP deflator is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 120. GDP deflator = (nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100 = (1,500 ÷ 1,250) × 100 = 120. 83.3 inverts the ratio; 250 is the difference, not a ratio.

questions.stem_md: A dyeing unit in an imagined town releases waste into a river, and farmers downstream lose part of their crop. GDP does not subtract this loss. This is an example of

options.text_md: a non-monetary exchange
a negative externality
a transfer payment
double counting

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a negative externality. A harm done to others for which no one pays is a negative externality, and GDP ignores it. Non-monetary exchanges are unpaid production, transfers are one-sided payments, and double counting is a measurement error.

questions.stem_md: Nominal GDP of an economy rises by 8 per cent while real GDP does not change. What has happened?

options.text_md: Physical output has risen by 8 per cent
The population has grown by 8 per cent
The general price level has risen; physical output is the same
Welfare has risen by 8 per cent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The general price level has risen; physical output is the same. Real GDP holds prices constant, so unchanged real GDP means unchanged output. The whole rise in nominal GDP is due to higher prices. It tells us nothing about population or welfare.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A rise in real GDP may not raise the welfare of most people in a country.

**Reason (R):** The extra output may go mainly to a small section of the population.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: if the distribution of income becomes more unequal, most people may not be better off even though real GDP rises.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cooking, cleaning and caring for children done by family members without payment are not counted in GDP, even though they add to welfare.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Such services are non-monetary and are hard to value, so GDP leaves them out; this is why GDP understates welfare.

questions.stem_md: An imagined economy's nominal GDP is ₹3,300 crore and its real GDP is ₹2,750 crore. Calculate the GDP deflator.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: GDP deflator = (nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100.
Step 2: (3,300 ÷ 2,750) × 100 = 120.

questions.stem_md: Nominal GDP of an imagined country is ₹6,480 crore and the GDP deflator is 120. Find real GDP (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Real GDP = (nominal GDP ÷ deflator) × 100.
Step 2: (6,480 ÷ 120) × 100 = 5,400. So ₹5,400 crore.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between nominal GDP and real GDP. Which is a better measure of growth in output?
questions.solution_md: Current vs base-year prices; real GDP removes the effect of price changes.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nominal GDP** values the output of a year at **current-year prices**; **real GDP** values it at **base-year (constant) prices**. **Real GDP** is better for comparing output over time, because it rises only when the **quantity** of goods and services rises, not when prices rise.

questions.stem_md: With one example each, explain how positive and negative externalities make GDP a poor measure of welfare.
questions.solution_md: One example of each and the direction in which GDP misstates welfare.

answer.model_answer_md: A **positive externality** is a benefit to others with no payment, e.g. a family's garden that cools the street; it raises welfare but is **not added** to GDP. A **negative externality** is a harm with no payment, e.g. **smoke** from a brick kiln harming neighbours; it lowers welfare but is **not subtracted**.

questions.stem_md: "A higher GDP means the people of a country are better off." Do you agree? Give three reasons for your answer.
questions.solution_md: A clear position with three reasons: distribution, non-monetary exchanges and externalities.

answer.model_answer_md:
Only **partly**. 1. **Distribution:** if the extra income goes to a few rich people, most people may be **no better off**.
2. **Non-monetary exchanges:** unpaid housework and barter in villages are **not counted**, so GDP misses part of welfare.
3. **Externalities:** pollution and congestion that come with output **reduce welfare**, but GDP does not subtract them.

questions.stem_md: An imagined state reports that its real GDP grew by 9 per cent in a year. Its finance minister claims that welfare has grown by the same amount. Evaluate this claim.
questions.solution_md: Give the case for, the three limitations, and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **For the claim:** real GDP measures more **goods and services** at constant prices, which can mean more food, housing and services, so welfare **may** rise.
2. **Distribution:** if most of the growth went to a **few** people, the welfare of the majority may hardly change.
3. **Non-monetary exchanges:** unpaid work at home and in villages is **not measured**, so GDP growth can even replace unpaid work with paid work without any gain in welfare.
4. **Externalities:** growth that brings **pollution** or ill health lowers welfare, but GDP does not subtract it.
5. **Judgement:** real GDP growth is a **useful but incomplete** index of welfare; the claim of an equal rise is too strong.
